bibliography.abstract: The public housing programme of the hegemonic government Housing and Development Board (HDB) has long occupied a central place within the ‘Singapore Story’ – the official foundation-narrative propagated by the Singaporean nation-state under the unbroken rule of the People’s Action Party (PAP) since 1959. In recent years, however, this narrative has increasingly been questioned by a range of scholars, writing from various perspectives. This article complements and supplements those authors’ revisionist accounts with the granular primary evidence contained in a little-known trove of archival housing files relating to the early years of PAP government. It focuses on the role of architects and planners within the dirigiste PAP-HDB system, highlighting that system’s opportunistic avoidance of demarcation-boundaries between built-environment professionals, mainstream civil servants and politicians. The article’s three-part structure reflects the turbulent fluctuations of the inaugural period of PAP rule. The first section, ‘Deconstruction’, briefly traces the role of housing and planning within the final breakdown of the colonial order in the mid/late 1950s. The two following sections, ‘Stabilization’ and ‘Reconstruction’, show how the HDB, and its architect-planners in particular, first re-embedded and then radically recast the housing system, and architectural ‘modernism’, in the service of the postcolonial regime that succeeded it.
bibliography.title: First decade revisited: architect-planners, public housing and the decolonization of Singapore

en.caveats: The study relies on a single, specific archival trove focused on the early PAP administration, which may limit its perspective on broader public reception or alternative planning voices of the era.
en.what: This study analyzes a little-known archive of primary housing files from the early years of Singapore's People's Action Party (PAP) government to trace the evolution of public housing from the late 1950s through the 1960s. It details how the Housing and Development Board (HDB) dissolved professional boundaries between architect-planners, civil servants, and politicians to build a highly centralized, dirigiste housing system. The analysis is structured across three phases: the deconstruction of the colonial planning order, the stabilization of the new system, and the reconstruction of architectural modernism to serve the postcolonial state.
en.why: It provides granular archival evidence that challenges the official state-propagated 'Singapore Story' of public housing, demonstrating that the HDB's success relied on an opportunistic blurring of professional and political boundaries rather than a clean, technocratic execution.
